summary:
Novgorod Oblast stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation, and no oblast-level deviation from that framework has been sourced. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression for Russia (June 2025), the note this division is scored against, contains no division-specific information beyond the national position, and the Human Rights Watch reporting used to calibrate enforcement carries no Novgorod-specific figures. The oblast is therefore assessed at the national score.

Consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised in Russia. Same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, so a trans visitor cannot obtain corrected identity documents or marriage-based partner status. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were prohibited outright in 2023, when the law banning gender reassignment surgery and legal changes of gender on official documents took effect; trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned the same year.

The Supreme Court designated the international LGBT+ movement an extremist organisation in November 2023. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for participation in that movement or for displaying its symbols as of 30 June 2025, with defendants facing up to 12 years in prison, and separately documented 81 people found guilty in 98 cases since January 2024 of administrative offences under article 20.3 for displaying banned LGBT symbols, mostly on social media.

Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement. Penalties under the propaganda statutes include fines of up to 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) or 15 days' detention for individuals, and the expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression that justifies gender transition. Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, detention and deportation, and official national government warnings state this explicitly to LGBT travellers. The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is at Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

Enforcement has grown in volume as well as severity. Cases under the propaganda laws have increased eighteenfold over the past decade, and fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles into the state budget in the two years preceding June 2025. Within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's extremist designation, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where around 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night. The Moscow Times reported on 23 June 2025 that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, and the Associated Press reported in December 2024 that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 that a transgender woman was lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

The UK Home Office note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims. Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.
tangentialFactors:
No oblast-level enforcement data for Novgorod Oblast has been sourced: the Human Rights Watch counts of 101 extremism convictions and 98 administrative cases are national aggregates, and the UK Home Office note records no division-specific detail. Absence of oblast-specific figures is a gap in the sourcing, not evidence of lower enforcement.

The escalation pattern documented nationally has been rapid rather than gradual. Fines under the propaganda statutes supplied more than 60 million rubles to the state budget in two years, and the post-designation raids in Moscow followed within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling, a tempo that bears on how quickly conditions can change anywhere in the country.

The conversion-therapy detention near Novosibirsk and the pretrial death of a detainee in December 2024 occurred outside Novgorod Oblast but illustrate the coercive treatment and detention risk available to authorities nationwide. Chechnya is cited in the UK Home Office note as a point of comparison for severity of persecution within the same national framework.

Russia's position differs from neighbouring jurisdictions where consensual same-sex activity is lawful and, in several cases, legal gender recognition is available, so a trans visitor arriving from such a jurisdiction should not expect those protections to travel with them.

outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Novgorod Oblast police or courts have conducted extremism or article 20.3 proceedings is unresolved; no oblast-level case data appears in the sourced inventory, and the national totals have not been broken down by division.

It is not sourced whether any LGBTQ-friendly venues in Novgorod or elsewhere in the oblast have been raided, or whether local authorities have issued oblast-level directives implementing the 2023 laws beyond the national statutes.

Access to what remains of transition-related medical care within the oblast after the 2023 healthcare ban is not sourced; the inventory establishes the national prohibition but gives no local service picture.

The reported figures for anti-LGBT+ enforcement differ in scope between sources (139 affected individuals for 2022–2024 in the UK Home Office note against 101 convictions and 98 administrative cases in Human Rights Watch reporting), and the inventory does not reconcile these counting methods.
